articles.title: In It, Pennywise the clown is a powerful metaphor for OCD
articles.author: Aisleen Sturrock, PhD Student in Creative Writing, Aberystwyth University
paras: Monsters are often used to represent mental health struggles, in both literature and film. These creatures often act as physical stand-ins for internal battles, giving shape to feelings that are usually invisible and hard to explain. By turning psychological distress into something audiences can see and react to, writers and filmmakers make those experiences easier to understand.

In the It franchise, the central monster is Pennywise the clown. In my research I seek to challenge the trivialisation of OCD by portraying the fear and complexity of living with the condition – and to deepen understanding of OCD themes through prose. While Stephen King’s original 1986 novel includes a complex mythology, I have found that the 2017 and 2019 film adaptations simplify Pennywise into a figure that works surprisingly well as a metaphor for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).

OCD is a condition in which a person experiences intense intrusive thoughts, known as obsessions. In response, people with OCD perform repetitive behaviours or mental acts called compulsions, to reduce distress or prevent a feared outcome. OCD can manifest itself through a range of different themes, often focusing on what someone values or fears most. For example, a person might worry they are a bad person because they dwell on a moment when they were slightly rude, or fear that stepping on a crack could harm a family member.

Eddie Kaspbrak, one of the main protagonists of King’s novel, experiences these kinds of compulsions. He has an intense fear of germs and illness that leads to a strong need for cleanliness, which he believes will prevent him from getting severe diseases.
This article is part of Rethinking the Classics. The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

Eddie fits with one of the most recognisable sub-types of the condition: contamination. This is a form of OCD in which someone believes that something has become contaminated by germs, illness, or even moral impurity such as sin. In response, they may engage in compulsive behaviour like frequent hand-washing, excessive cleaning of surfaces, or avoiding places and people they perceive as contaminated.

Played by Bill Skarsgård in the films It (2017) and It Chapter Two (2019), Pennywise’s strength builds from his ability to get into people’s heads. He feeds off the fear that grows through obsessions and remuneration. Remuneration is a compulsion in which a person repeatedly engages with intrusive thoughts, analysing them in an attempt to understand or resolve them. However this often makes the OCD cycle worse.
In It, the more the victim dwells on the fear, the stronger Pennywise becomes. This is similar to the way that when someone with OCD gives into their compulsions, their symptoms worsen.

Pennywise changes shape to match each child’s deepest fear. As the children become more frightened, he grows larger and more threatening. This mirrors the OCD cycle, where fear and avoidance reinforce intrusive thoughts, making them feel increasingly real and impossible to ignore.

In It: Chapter Two, Mike (Isaiah Mustafa) – one of the original frightened children, now a grown man – suggests that Pennywise knows “what scares [children] the most” and uses it to “salt the meat”. In both the film and novel, Pennywise appeared to Eddie as a diseased leper, directly targeting his intense fear of illness and contamination.

In the novel, Eddie experiences intrusive thoughts in his mother’s voice, something he calls his “mind-mother”. Eddie remembers his mother telling him he is “not like other people” and has “a very weak system,” reinforcing the idea that he is always at risk. Even after her death, her fears about sickness continue to control his behaviour. These internal warnings eventually become absurd in their extremity – “Eddie, get out of the taxi! They give you cancer!” – highlighting the exaggerated, catastrophic thinking typical of contamination OCD.

If Eddie’s mother’s voice represents his intrusive thoughts, then his inhaler (or his “aspirator”) is his compulsion. Even though, as an adult, he knows his inhaler was only ever a placebo, he still uses it in moments of stress. The irrationality of his fear doesn’t make it feel any less real.

In the novel, Eddie’s inhaler is repeatedly linked to violent imagery. In one section of the book, it is described like a weapon. Eddie stuffs it into his mouth and, “like miming suicide”, pulls “the trigger”. This unsettling comparison highlights how compulsions, while meant to provide relief, are harmful.

Later in the novel, Eddie’s compulsion of using his inhaler, meant to provide mental relief, is personified as a cruel voice that threatens him: “this time I might just kill ya!” This suggests that compulsions can become as frightening as the intrusive thoughts they are meant to control. Even knowing this, Eddie instinctively reaches for the inhaler, trapped in the familiar cycle of fear and temporary relief.
Eddie fights Pennywise and OCD

During the novel’s climax, Eddie turns his inhaler into a weapon against Pennywise, aiming it at the creature’s eyes. As he does, he imagines his mother’s voice warning him: “Don’t go near that Thing, Eddie! Things like that give you cancer!” This moment is important because Eddie doesn’t obey the intrusive thought – he challenges it. By using the object of his compulsion as a tool of resistance, Eddie symbolically pushes back against both his mother’s control and his disorder.

The final confrontation in the film adaptation It: Chapter Two (2019) also reflects real therapeutic ideas. Unlike in the novel, Pennywise isn’t defeated through brute force, but through psychological resistance.

The “losers” (as the kids describe themselves) insult and mock him, calling him “just a clown”. As they do, Pennywise physically shrinks and loses power. This mirrors Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a therapy which encourages patients to let obsessions occur without completing the compulsion. Once Pennywise is no longer feared, he collapses, much like OCD loses its hold when compulsions are resisted.

It works as a striking metaphor for OCD. Each character is attacked through their deepest fears, and the more those fears are fixated on, the stronger Pennywise becomes. By turning intrusive thoughts into literal monsters, It captures the intensity of OCD’s internal struggles and offers a deeper, more empathetic understanding of the disorder and its emotional weight.

articles.title: Lucía Caminos is the first Latina ‘Grand Theft Auto’ lead – these video game characters paved the way
articles.author: Regina Marie Mills, Associate Professor of American Culture, University of Michigan
paras: If the Netflix-exclusive trailer that briefly crashed the streaming service in August 2026 is any indication, “Grand Theft Auto VI” – a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style crime saga set in a satirical, fictionalized Florida – may be the most anticipated video game of all time.

It’s been 13 years since gaming company Rockstar released a new title in its flagship franchise. Fans have spent years dissecting leaked footage, constructing elaborate theories about the game’s mechanics and even attempting to reconstruct its fictional map using real-world geography.

But as a Latino studies scholar who teaches and researches video games, I’m most excited by the fact that “Grand Theft Auto VI” is the first title in the series to feature a Latina lead character: Lucía Caminos.
Not everyone is thrilled about a female protagonist – sexism, after all, remains a persistent issue in the gaming community.

But it nonetheless represents a watershed moment, as Latina video game characters have historically played second fiddle. Latino popular culture scholar Frederick Luis Aldama has pointed out how Latinos usually exist as obstacles for players to overcome rather than heroes whose stories players get to experience firsthand.

At the same time, a host of Latina characters throughout video game history – some playable, most not – paved the way for Lucía. Together, they show how representation is less about skin color and more about connection, complexity and character development.
A ‘badass Latina’ who travels the world
In 1985, Carmen Sandiego was introduced as a criminal mastermind in “Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?”
Players must pursue Carmen as she leaves a trail of clues across the globe. But Brøderbund, the game’s developer, left Carmen’s ethnic identity and origins ambiguous.

While researching the Brøderbund Collection at the Strong Museum of Play, I learned that the game’s creators originally imagined Carmen as a man named Estaban Devious who was born in Andorra, a tiny country in the Pyrenees with a large Spanish-speaking population. Brøderbund eventually settled on Carmen Sandiego – a name deemed exotic and befitting of a world traveler.

Despite Carmen’s unclear origins, Latinas have long connected with her. Actress Gina Rodriguez was so taken with Carmen as a kid that she jumped at the chance to voice Carmen in the animated series “Carmen Sandiego,” which premiered on Netflix in 2019 and ran for four seasons. According to Rodriguez, Carmen was “an incredible, strong, feminist, badass Latina who was going around the world. … I wanted to be just like her.” This cartoon gave Carmen a clear backstory – she was Argentine – and complicated her portrayal as a villain by having her turn on the very criminal organization she once belonged to.

With the show introducing Carmen Sandiego to a new generation of kids, new titles continue to appear. To coincide with Carmen’s 40th anniversary, “Carmen Sandiego” was released in 2025. It finally makes Carmen a playable character.
Like Carmen Sandiego, Isabela Keyes is a villain. One of the antagonists of the 2006 game “Dead Rising,” Isabela is the sister of Carlito Keyes, who initiates a zombie outbreak in Colorado.

Players discover that Isabela and Carlito infected people with the zombie virus to avenge the destruction of their hometown, Santa Cabeza, a fictional Central American village. The U.S. government had been experimenting with the virus there and destroyed the town to cover up its research.
But Isabela eventually realizes that she and Carlito have gone too far. She has a change of heart and ends up turning against her brother.

I think of Isabela as an important Latina video game character because she’s not simply included as a pretty face. That’s too often been the case for Latina characters, whether it’s Cynthia Velasquez in “Silent Hill 4” – whose alternate costume in the game made her look like a Playboy bunny – or Katarina Alves in “Tekken 7,” whose default and alternate costumes prominently feature her thong.

Capcom, the studio that produced the game, nonetheless marketed Isabela as a sex symbol. The question of how to interpret this sort of sexualization has divided gamers and scholars. On the one hand, many game designers still see their target audience as heterosexual men. However, women now make up half the gaming market, and overtly sexualized characters, which continue to appear, could further the sexism that bedevils the industry.
Video games have historically featured few queer characters, let alone queer Latino characters.

But indie games, which are developed outside major studios and often prioritize creative experimentation over commercial conventions, have generally been more welcoming to LGBTQ+ narratives and representation.

Fullbright’s 2013 exploration game “Gone Home” tells a 1990s coming-out story. Players explore the empty Oregon home of Katie Greenbriar and gradually learn the story of her younger sister, Sam, and Sam’s Mexican American girlfriend, Lonnie DeSoto, who hopes to one day join the military.

Though Lonnie is not a playable character, players piece together her experiences through letters and other clues. They learn about the challenges Lonnie faces as a Latina lesbian in the Junior Reserve Officers Training Corps, a high school program that teaches military-style leadership and discipline. By incorporating aspects of 1990s zine culture, the U.S. military’s Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell policy toward homosexuality and the feminist punk movement Riot Grrrl, “Gone Home” accurately and realistically captured the hopes and fears of being LGBTQ+ in the 1990s.
Getting a chance to play Latina

For years, playable Latina characters were pretty much nonexistent. Opportunities almost exclusively came from the large rosters of fighting games – characters like Ángel in the 2001 game “King of Fighters” and Christie Monteiro in “Tekken,” also released in 2001.
Over the past decade, that’s started to change.

Sombra is a Mexican hacker and one of the most prominent characters in the 2016 futuristic shooter “Overwatch.” Born Olivia Colomar, she was orphaned as a child and grew up in Mexico, where she developed extraordinary computer skills. She works with the game’s antagonists but pursues her own agenda of unraveling a global conspiracy.

Zyanya Mondragón, better known as Reyna, is a Mexican character in the 2020 futuristic shooter “VALORANT.” Reyna is a supernatural warrior who absorbs the life energy of enemies she kills, using it to heal herself and grow stronger. But her bloodthirsty nature has a deeply personal motivation: She needs the life energy she harvests to keep her younger sister, Lucia, alive.

These two characters have compelling pasts and aren’t clear-cut antagonists. However, they still sometimes fall victim to the “sexy Latina” stereotype. For example, in a segment of Conan O'Brien’s Clueless Gamer series, in which the blundering comedian tries out new video games, O'Brien repeatedly ogles over Sombra’s body.

Lucía Caminos will join just a handful of playable Latina characters, like Kait Diaz from “Gears of War,” in what are known as “AAA games” – titles with the biggest marketing and development budgets. But unlike the “Gears of War” franchise, which was Xbox-only on release, “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be released simultaneously on PlayStation 5, Xbox and the PC.

Yes, Lucía Caminos is an attractive young woman who breaks the law. But richly developed video game characters can move beyond stereotypes and give players new ways to imagine marginalized people as heroes. Rather than judging characters like Lucía as examples of either good or bad representation, it might be better to think about how players can reinterpret their stories, see them as role models and identify with their struggles.
After all, gamers have been doing just that since Carmen Sandiego.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is James Bond – an unexpected choice that bodes well for the next era of 007
articles.author: James Chapman, Professor of Film Studies, University of Leicester
paras: Speculation over the next 007 has been fervent ever since Daniel Craig announced his departure after his fifth outing as the spy in No Time to Die (2021). That search has now ended with 40-year-old British actor Robert Pattinson confirmed as the new James Bond.

The intensity of the guessing game is a testament both to the public’s enduring fascination Bond and to the expectations that now rest on Pattinson’s shoulders as the longest-running continuous series in cinema history moves into a new era at Amazon Studios.
For Amazon, the drawn-out casting process has generated valuable free publicity at a time when there was no real news about Bond 26.

Unlike previous Bond castings, this one has been played out on social media, aided by our 24-hour news cycle, with its insatiable appetite for content. In 2024 several reputable media outlets ran with a story that Aaron Taylor-Johnson was about to be announced as the new Bond. That proved to be a false dawn – albeit rather more plausible than the hoax announcement that Australian model Finlay Light had been cast in 1986. Most recently, Josh O'Connor and Callum Turner appeared to be among the strongest contenders.
Pattinson will be only the seventh actor to play Bond on the big screen in 65 years. Inevitably there will be comparisons with his predecessors.
For many fans, Sean Connery remains the original and best, incarnating the suave but ruthless secret agent with a licence to kill in seven pictures from Dr No (1962) to Never Say Never Again (1983).

Connery was the only actor whom Bond’s creator Ian Fleming met, and contrary to popular belief, the author approved of the casting. He wrote in a letter that “the man they have chosen for Bond, Sean Connery, is a real charmer – fairly unknown but a good actor with the right looks and physique”.

When Connery stepped down for the first time, following You Only Live Twice (1967), Australian model George Lazenby, the only Bond actor who can genuinely be described as “unknown”, was a one-off Bond in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969). But it was Roger Moore, at the time one of the biggest television stars in the world (after roles in The Saint and The Persuaders!), who made a lighter but popular replacement in seven continuous films, from Live and Let Die (1973) to A View to a Kill (1985).
Arguably the best actor to play Bond, the classically trained Timothy Dalton, was a late replacement for Pierce Brosnan, tied to a contract for a cancelled television show in 1986.

Dalton’s performance remains the closest psychologically to Fleming’s character, although his tenure lasted only two films. The announcement of Brosnan’s casting for GoldenEye (1995) came as no surprise and in the decade since he “lost” the role, he had matured into it. Brosnan successfully restored the popular appeal of the Bond series in four films until Die Another Day (2002).
And then came Craig, a controversial choice for being “too short” and “too blonde”, who proved the naysayers wrong in five box-office blockbusters from Casino Royale (2006) to No Time to Die (2021).

In certain respects, the casting of Pattinson seems a left-field choice, just as Craig’s was. His name was a late addition to the shortlist of candidates leaked (or, possibly, trailed to gauge public opinion) over recent weeks.

Pattinson also differs from all the other Bonds in having box-office pedigree from mainstream movie franchises, including Edward Cullen in the Twilight saga and Batman in The Batman (2022). If this suggests safety-first casting for Amazon, we should bear in mind that Pattinson has also done his share of edgy, independent films with directors including David Cronenberg and Werner Herzog.

I expect there’ll be some kickback online, as there was with Craig. Bond fans can be extremely territorial about “their” hero. But Pattinson has a lot going for him. He’s the right sort of age: James Bond is an experienced agent who requires some maturity and gravitas. He’s tall and good looking in a slightly odd sort of way, perhaps suggesting something of the “alien and un-English” quality that Fleming identified in his hero. And Pattinson showed that he had something “Bondian” about him in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet (2020).

An important point I take away from this news, given the widely-aired concern that Amazon don’t properly understand the Bond franchise, is that Pattinson’s casting indicates the studio is going to maintain Bond’s essential Britishness.

With Denis Villeneuve in the director’s chair and Peaky Blinders’ Stephen Knight writing the script, the next Bond picture will be another reset for the series. I think Amazon have made a good call. This will be a new dawn, not twilight, for James Bond.

articles.title: Why freelance culture in the media makes it so hard for women to report abuse
articles.author: Emily Coleman, Lecturer in Creative Industries, The Open University
paras: In the conviction of Russell Brand and the Metropolitan police’s announcement that it has launched an investigation into David Walliams over separate allegations of serious sexual offences, the media industries have come under renewed scrutiny over how workplace cultures enable misconduct and abuse.

The two cases stand at very different legal stages. Brand has been convicted and jailed after a court found he exploited a culture of deference to talent to abuse women with impunity. Walliams has not been arrested or charged, and strongly denies all allegations of criminal behaviour or wrongdoing. He maintains that past relationships with women he met through his public profile were consensual, though he has admitted behaving “thoughtlessly”.

But what about the women working in the media industries who were targets of workplace misconduct and abuse? What made them particularly vulnerable to assault, what prevented them from speaking out and why was it so difficult for those who did to have their stories taken seriously?

My research investigates the media industries and creative work, so I am interested in how working environments make women vulnerable to abuse, while also making it professionally risky to challenge the behaviour of people in positions of power.

Four of the six women who testified against Russell Brand during his trial worked for TV or radio organisations. Some of the assaults happened in the workplace, where Brand felt confident his behaviour would go unchallenged.

One woman – who the prosecution barrister described as “just a woman trying to get on with her work” – was kissed and groped by Brand in front of his entourage. Another was working on a Channel 4 project when Brand asked her to give him a massage and put his head in her crotch, while two male colleagues looked on and laughed.

According to the Telegraph, a junior colleague at Walliams’ publisher HarperCollins raised a complaint in 2023 about alleged inappropriate behaviour. The paper reported that no formal action was taken against Walliams – who has denied wrongdoing – while the woman was given a five-figure settlement, signed a non-disclosure agreement and left the company. HarperCollins only parted ways with Walliams two years later, following a change in management.

During Brand’s trial, his defence barrister repeatedly questioned why the women didn’t speak out at the time, in some cases, waiting decades after the crimes were committed to come forward. There are many barriers to reporting sexual violence, including shame, self-blame, the low rate of successful prosecutions and the prospect of hostile questioning in court. But many reasons why women remain silent are also rooted in the circumstances of their working lives.

Media production is a predominantly freelance industry. Creative workers are typically employed on short-term contracts, moving from one company to the next. In a highly competitive workplace, professional reputation is a form of currency. Being perceived as difficult or troublesome can be a red flag. Workers are hired through informal recruitment networks that are not open to scrutiny and may never know the reason why the phone suddenly stops ringing.
One of Brand’s victims told the court she didn’t complain at the time because she had a mortgage to pay. Another said: “I thought it was my word against his and he was a big famous asset.”

For women in the industry, workplace pressures are compounded by gender inequalities. Research shows that marginalised workers are less able to endure challenging conditions. In an industry where women outnumber men at entry level, evidence shows a mid-career exodus, with many female workers leaving the industry before they are able to progress into senior roles.

But sometimes the women who were abused did speak out. In some cases they complained to line managers, colleagues and HR departments who took little effective action. Formal complaints about Brand’s sexual misconduct were made to the BBC in 2019, yet it was only after allegations were brought to public attention by a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches programme that the Met Police began an investigation, which the BBC later acknowledged.
Following Brand’s conviction, culture secretary Lisa Nandy has told the media industries that their “time is up” to put systems in place to protect people who speak out against abuse.

Nandy has urged organisations to sign up to the new Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, which has launched an independent whistleblowing service to encourage greater accountability. But reporting mechanisms are, by their nature, retrospective and not designed to prevent harm from happening in the first place.

Meanwhile, insecure freelance work, informal recruitment practices and ingrained power hierarchies continue to create conditions in which speaking out carries professional risk and make the media industries an unsafe workplace for women.
Emily Coleman receives funding from the Arts & Humanities Research Council and the Economic & Social Research Council.

articles.title: Mogging is the word of the year – but men have been doing it since Shakespearean times
articles.author: Oliver Lewis, Lecturer in Early Modern Literature, King's College London
paras: The Collins English Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year.

The Collins website says that the word originated with the acronym AMOG – or “alpha male of the group” – which is often associated with bodybuilding forums and, more recently, the toxic culture of incels and the manosphere. But mogging has now entered mainstream language with its meaning slightly repurposed: to describe someone who is outperforming, outshining or upstaging someone.

While the verb is often used in reference to physical looks, it can also be applied in other contexts. Alex Beecroft, managing director of Collins, explained that the selection of mogging demonstrates how “each generation leaves its mark on language”, with the term seeing a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.

The Oxford English Dictionary contains four historic meanings of the base verb “mog”. The earliest meaning and usage comes as early as 1674, referring to card games “to exchange a card with the dealer”. A later usage means “to move on, depart, decamp”. By the mid-1800s, two new possible meanings emerged: “to walk slowly but steadily” and “to shift (a person, animal etc.) to cause to move on (esp. quickly)”.

What unites these historic meanings is the connection to movement or performance. For many men in the early modern period, the demonstration of superiority through action and movement was a key method to showcase, or perhaps fittingly, “mog” others.

New research by theatre historian Eleanor Rycroft explores this link between movement, gender and social power. Rycroft examines theatrical works by playwrights such as Shakespeare and Ben Jonson alongside historical conduct books and household management guides, revealing just how much cultural capital was attached to a man’s posture and stride.

How-to guides and etiquette books from the time told men and women how to behave, labelling certain traits as respectable and others as improper. In the 1566 English translation of Ortensio Landi’s Delectable Demaundes and Pleasaunt Questions (1566), readers were shown how to outdo other men in wit and conduct. Yet in doing so, the text also exposed the cracks in this ideal, revealing how precarious that masculine status truly was.

In his influential Book of the Courtier (1528), courtier and diplomat Baldassare Castiglione defined this quality as a “certain nonchalance, which shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought”.
Sprezzatura in Shakespeare and asserting manhood
Castiglione was first translated into English by Sir Thomas Hoby in 1561, and the concept of sprezzatura heavily influenced early modern English culture.

In many early modern plays, characters demonstrate the importance of asserting a mastery of manhood and, with it, upstaging others. While Shakespeare does not use the terms sprezzatura or mogging in any of his works, many men attempt to outperform or outshine other characters to assert or affirm their manly status.

In Much Ado About Nothing (first performed 1598), the “merry war” between protagonists Beatrice and Benedick – a rapid-fire exchange loaded with insults as the two characters shield their true feelings for one another – is often a source of audience amusement and laughter. However, this “skirmish of wit” points to the different expectations on men and women for Benedick across the play text: to match and ideally best Beatrice’s skill in wordplay so as not to emasculate himself.

Beatrice seems to be aware of these dynamics of masculinity, noting that Benedick “gets nothing” from their verbal exchanges – after their last encounter, “four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one”. These scenes of verbal sparring might be understood as a trial of masculinity, testing Benedick’s skills in rhetoric and wordplay.

A more direct trial is captured in the penultimate scene of Shakespeare’s Henry IV Part 1 (first performed in 1597), which depicts the showdown between Prince Hal, who will eventually ascend to be Henry V and Henry Percy, known as Harry Hotspur, a young yet accomplished knight who rebels against King Henry IV.

Both men recognise that the ultimate upstaging, trial by combat, would result in the consolidation of manhood and admirable reputation for one man, and the death and diminished reputation of the other. Hal notes that “two stars keep not their motion in one sphere, nor can one England brook a double reign”. Both men cannot coexist and claim to upstage one another.

The irony of modern “mogging” lies in how self-conscious it has become. Where Castiglione’s sprezzatura demanded that dominance appear effortless and natural, today’s digital posturing often betrays the very insecurity it tries to hide.

Collins may have christened “mogging” a defining term of our contemporary moment, but the performance itself is a familiar historical echo – men working hard to make looking superior appear easy and natural.

articles.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled: why meeting TV rules isn’t enough to protect reality show participants
articles.author: Helen Wood, Professor in Media and Cultural Studies, Aston University
paras: Channel 4 has announced its decision to cancel the reality TV show Married at First Sight UK (Mafs UK). It is the show that saw couples matched by relationship experts who were then wed in faux commitment ceremonies upon meeting for the first time.

The cancellation is the result of a BBC Panorama investigation in May 2026 which drew, among other sources, upon research by myself and colleagues at ReCARETV. Our project comprises more than 120 interviews with broadcasting executives, commissioners, production workers and reality TV participants.

The Panorama investigation highlighted accounts from former Mafs UK participants who came forward to journalists and our research team with allegations of sexual assault and misconduct during production. Even with strict anonymity protections in place, many still found it difficult to speak to us. Often, reality television participants do not realise that signing a confidentiality clause does not legally prevent them from speaking out about harm.

Change happens when people are finally heard and believed. Yet this places enormous pressure on already traumatised people to articulate their experiences and fit their narratives into available avenues for complaint. Having listened to these accounts, and heard their fears that others will suffer the same harm, Channel 4’s decision to end the show is a welcome step.

Yet, I wonder how that decision to cancel Mafs UK can be squared with the findings of Channel 4’s external reviews. Shared with the public on November 5, the reports found that the show did not break Ofcom’s broadcasting code and that it could “reasonably continue” with some extra measures in place.

For someone who experienced severe harm during production, waiting for Channel 4’s reports only to hear that the broadcaster’s practices met expected standards is potentially re-traumatising. Learning that the show could have continued would have made this harder to bear.
Compliance and responsibility

My ReCARETV colleagues and I have spent the last three years researching care in reality and unscripted TV production (our final report From Compliance to Care, is forthcoming). To us, it is not surprising that the show’s protocols were found to be compliant with the code.

This demonstrates that an emphasis on protocols, compliance and robust paperwork is not enough to protect people from harm. Our research shows that the realities of television production – specifically a fast-paced drive for drama and the conditions of a precarious, freelance workforce – frequently undermine these intentions.

The reasonable measures that are mentioned in the external review of Mafs UK for Channel 4 include installing CCTV in all rooms, the use of safe words and extra lockable bolts on bedrooms and bathrooms, among other suggestions which aim to take the pressure off the risks of intimacy.
Presumably, if Channel 4’s decision is still to cancel the show, this is because Mafs UK is now either too difficult to make, or changes would sufficiently diminish its popularity.

It seems that these responses to compliance and new safety measures disavow any acknowledgement that the show’s high pressure in production around sexual intimacy was essentially unsafe. Once again the TV industry is resisting any reasonable understanding of harm and reinforcing the exceptionalism of TV as a space where boundaries are pushed in the interests of creative freedom.

Ofcom’s response after waiting for the Channel 4 reviews has been to offer more guidance to which broadcasters should “have regard”. These include some welcome considerations such as a more developed model of ongoing consent, allowing participants some access to family and friends away from the show and ensuring that background checks are completed in time.

These are all recommendations my research colleagues and I welcome and are supported by findings in our data that were shared with Ofcom over the summer. But the Ofcom guidance also introduces something new which is the mention of the “conduct” of participants. Our research suggests that participants are regularly issued codes of conduct on reality shows and the external Channel 4 report suggests heavier sanctions for participants breaking such codes. This sends a message about participants’ own responsibility.

Our research shows a major flaw in how duty-of-care compliance is sometimes built. Too often, it becomes a tick-box exercise designed to shield broadcasters from complaints, rather than protect participants from harm.

The ReCARETV research found that a common practice in reality TV is the so-called “talk of doom”, in which mental health professionals warn participants of worst-case scenarios to secure their consent. Rather than helping contributors understand how production and editing actually work, this approach shifts responsibility from the broadcaster onto the individual. Similarly, our concern with how the industry and regulators have responded to the trauma on Mafs UK is that they disperse responsibility for the harm, rather than owning it directly.

Ofcom, as a post-broadcast regulator, cannot offer any compensation to participants even if their complaint is upheld. There is still no formal space to protect participants who take part in reality shows.

My research colleagues and I welcome the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, which is now formally recognised in Parliament as the independent whistleblowing body for film, TV, music and theatre – and the first to formally recognise reality TV participants within the creative industries. Still, change cannot rely only on people speaking out. The industry must also confront its own systemic failures and accept ethical responsibility.
The question should not just be about whether a show is compliant, but whether it is ethical, safe and humane.

articles.title: Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury looks beyond the sex to the art – with mixed results
articles.author: Benedict Carpenter van Barthold, Lecturer, School of Art & Design, Nottingham Trent University
paras: The originality of painters Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant is often sensationalised, with the focus being on their unconventional sex lives as much as their avant-garde art.

The pair were members of the informal Bloomsbury group, a loose constellation of gilded artists, writers and intellectuals centred around Gordon Square in central London. The group is coarsely remembered as much for its triangular romantic liaisons as its cultural contributions.

A new survey at Tate Britain attempts to bring the focus back to the duo’s work. The first room of Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury is a cameo of what follows. A pair of portraits by Grant introduce the couple in their early association.
A dramatic self-portrait of the artist wearing a teal headscarf (1910), his right arm posed to frame his face, is matched by a portrait of Bell (1911-1912), vibrantly costumed in a yellow shawl.

Several of the paintings in this room show the pair working at the leading edge of artistic style. Vanessa Bell’s Self-Portrait of 1915, the hero image for the exhibition, feels particularly connected with Parisian art of the period, suggesting the influence of Henri Matisse.

Closing the narrative in this first room, two touching self-portraits of later life show the artists grown together in style and life. The posture and attire in these two works are mirrored, and the radical edge of their youthful expression is rounded, mellowed. Bell’s self-portrait was made two years after Grant’s, in about 1958. In this there is a sense of resignation or departure. She died three years later, predeceasing Grant by 17 years.
Dropping formalities and breaking norms
Grant was introduced to Bell (then Vanessa Stephen) in 1905, by his cousin, at a weekly painting salon.

Their relationship deepened in 1909 when Bell wrote to Grant, suggesting that they drop formalities and address each other by their first names. Even though Grant was gay, and Bell was by this point married, the pair entered a close personal and creative relationship that endured for five decades and produced a child – the writer and painter Angelica Garnett. During this period, they both had numerous lovers.

As the exhibition’s curator Thomas Kennedy told me: “I think people bring it down to sex, but actually it’s about freedom. It’s freedom from the Victorian traditional norms that they had that they felt had been imposed upon them. So, actually, they were looking at new ways of living, and freedom to love who you wanted.”

In Britain today these freedoms are protected by law, however circumscribed they may be by the contingencies of normal life. But throughout this show, whether considering Bell and Grant’s advanced artistic style or evidence of their unusual lives, it is the very earliness of their acts that makes them radical, not necessarily the acts themselves.

The first room establishes the show’s theme. The rest of the exhibition walks the viewer through the artists’ work in a broad chronology. At art school, we see Duncan precisely but superficially copying from the French master Jean Siméon Chardin, missing the metaphysical heart of Chardin’s greatness. By contrast, there are two lovely still lifes by Bell, the slightly maladroit Iceland Poppies (1908-9), and Apples: 46 Gordon Square (c. 1908-1909). These two paintings are squarely Edwardian, but they capture more than the mere appearance of their subjects.

In the words of Bell’s sister, the novelist Virginia Woolf, “human character changed”, when the painter and critic Roger Fry came into the ambit of the Bloomsbury group. Through Fry’s show Manet and the Post-Impressionists, which was staged in London at the Grafton Galleries in 1910, Bell and Grant absorbed the influence and experimental velocity of the European avant-garde.

What followed was a frenetic period of innovation. Two paintings by Vanessa Bell of Studland Beach show her style evolve from something received from Paul Gauguin into to a radical pared down abstraction, a study in form and colour. There are several works in this room that are among the earliest purely abstract British painting. Stylistically, Bell and Grant came early to modernism. But much of the experimental work in this show needs the context of its early date to feed its impact.

The pair were pivotal in the Omega workshops, a commercial endeavour started by Fry, which aimed at closing the false distinction between the fine and decorative arts. This ran out of steam within six years, in Fry’s words due to the “utter indifference … of the public”.

It produced a wealth of charming objects, several of which are presented in this show, including a pair of impishly joyous fans made of ivory and silk, painted by Grant. Despite the closure of the Omega workshops, the pair’s flair for space and colour found expression in other designs for the stage, and commissions for interiors.

One stand-out work is Famous Women Dinner Service (1932-34), commissioned from the pair by the patrician art historian Kenneth Clark. This joint work features 50 portraits of female luminaries including Jezebel, Cleopatra, Elizabeth Tudor, Miss 1933 and – oddly – both Bell and Grant.

Created 40 years before Judy Chicago’s more celebrated installation The Dinner Party, which features a table set in celebration of 39 famous women, for once Bell and Grant’s slightly bonkers feminist dinner service seems decades ahead of its time, rather than a beat behind.
There is one small room, painted dark purple, that is undeniably all Grant’s. It’s a display of his “very private” erotic drawings.

These unpolished sketches depict gay sex, much of it acrobatic. Many are created on the reverse of receipts or other scraps. Forty of them were exhibited at Charleston, the artists’ Sussex home and now a museum, as recently as three years ago. Other artistically meritorious works in the main body of the show are testament to Grant’s sexuality. In an exhibition that aims for an unsensationalised reappraisal of Grant and Bell’s shared work, a roomful of private drawings unintended for display is an unnecessary tangent.

The concluding room features a recreation of the pair’s shared studio at Charleston, a painstaking endeavour that was three years in the preparation. This feels like another stage set, and by this point in the show their presence as characters is well established.

Ultimately, the exhibition tells the story of two leading lights of the Edwardian intelligentsia, in contact with the key ideas of the European avant-garde, shaping a British modernity before turning to a cosseted introversion. Much of the early work is radical, and some of the later work is beautiful. Not all of it feels vital.
Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury runs from November 12 2026 to April 11 2027 at Tate Britain

articles.title: How to Rob a Bank asks whether a motive can ever justify a crime
articles.author: Edward White, Assistant lecturer in Psychology, Kingston University
paras: David Leitch’s heist thriller How to Rob a Bank sets out its to critique from its opening moments: in a world this socially and economically unequal, can the right motive make a crime OK?

The story follows a crew of social media-savvy bank robbers, Ringleader (Nicolas Hoult), Getaway Driver (Anna Sawai), Muscle (Pete Davidson) and Tech-guru (Rhenzy Feliz), who broadcast their raids and soon find the police chasing them. Every time the robbers commit a crime, they post about it. The public soon joins in, posting footage of crimes of their own. The robbery becomes almost secondary to the crew – the audience engagement and consumption of the content is their real prize.
So why are they doing this?

The robbers have each experienced hardship, from insurmountable healthcare costs and predatory banks to immigration enforcement. By robbing from the corrupt they are trying to level the playing field. Their “how to” videos intend to empower the downtrodden.

The robbers justify their actions through arguments about inequality, which the film treats as both a genuine grievance and an excuse. Throughout their videos, the crew quote statistics arguing that the bankers are the real criminals, the ones taking advantage of ordinary people.

This reflects strain theory, first set out by sociologist Robert Merton in 1938. It argues that crime becomes more likely when society promotes goals such as wealth while denying many people legitimate means of reaching them. Debt and capitalism sit in the background of the film as exactly that kind of system, and the film points at how debt is created and who profits from it.

The robbers are against those profiteers and attest to be firmly on the side of the people. For instance, in one video, the robbers coach viewers, telling them not to talk to the police when arrested and reminding them of their right to a lawyer. They note that the United States Supreme Court has held that officers can use deception to secure convictions.
Despite all this, How to Rob a Bank is wary of its “heroes”.

The criminals donate money to charities from the banks they rob, yet keep the lion’s share for themselves. In one heist, the crew hand out free iPads to the gathered masses, a distraction that doubles as a demonstration: the crowd scrambling for free devices is as hungry as the robbers.

Criminologists like Ray Surette have a name for this: performance crime. These are offences created for distribution on social media, performed for an audience rather than hidden from it. They are conducted for fame, notoriety and attention.

Despite increasing their personal wealth, the crew in How to Rob A Bank convince themselves that they are helping people. Sociologists Gresham Sykes and David Matza called such justifications techniques of neutralisation: the excuses offenders use to quiet their own moral code, from denying that anyone is really a victim to appealing to a higher loyalty. Generosity, like the iPads, becomes branding.

After all those murky motives, the film’s answer for what the best motive could be for committing a crime is disarmingly simple: love. Not ideology, not justice, but the people the robbers cannot bear to lose. However, love here works as a moat, not a bridge: it protects the robbers’ own and leaves everyone else outside.

Canadian-American psychologist Paul Bloom puts it more vividly, describing empathy as a spotlight that shines brightly on those we love and dims for everyone else. As a response to inequality, it shelters the few, not the many.

With a crowded crew to serve, the film hands each robber a motive and moves on, sketching where it should scrutinise. That leaves its case for love resting on people the audience barely knows: mouthpieces for social commentary rather than flesh-and-blood.

To be fair, this is a heist action film first and foremost. As film scholar Daryl Lee shows, the heist genre has always smuggled an anti-institutional message inside its capers – but the message rarely outweighs the thrill of the job. How to Rob a Bank was never going to dismantle capitalism between set pieces. Instead, it raises the big questions, then hands the homework to the audience.

articles.title: Cathy Come Home at 60: many of the housing issues the film exposed still exist today
articles.author: Jessica Field, Research Associate,  Humanitarian and Conflict Response Institute, University of Manchester
paras: “You don’t care. You only pretend to care!” an exhausted, homeless Cathy shouts at a board of welfare officials just days before her children are taken from her. It’s a scene from Cathy Come Home, the 1966 BBC drama that remains – 60 years on – a touchstone for discussions on homelessness.

Written by Jeremy Sandford and directed by Ken Loach, the television play follows Cathy and her husband Reg, who are expecting a child when Reg loses his income through injury. The couple then lose their home, the first of many instances of this. Eventually Cathy ends up, with three children in tow, at an overcrowded government hostel that doesn’t permit husbands. Cathy finally loses her children to the care system, leaving her broken and alone on a railway platform.

Despite its age, the film is recognised even by people who were not yet born when it was first screened. As recently as 2016, it spawned a new initiative: Homes for Cathy, a network of housing associations and charities kickstarted to “end homelessness”.

Studies have highlighted controversy and debate as key to cementing the film’s cultural status. Though the main cast were actors, Loach employed groundbreaking techniques to present a composite of things that had genuinely happened to people over the preceding 18 months.

He filmed in real locations, used improvised dialogue and captured authentic encounters between the couple and gatekeepers to housing – people like landlords. A narrator also listed facts about housing poverty over the visuals. One of the most damning statistics from the time hangs as text over the closing frame: “4,000 children are separated from their parents and taken into care each year because their parents are homeless.”

For decades, media and government figures argued about the veracity of the statistics, how accurate Cathy’s experience was and whether it was right to blend fact and fiction in this way. The ordinariness of fact-based drama today (things like Mr Bates vs The Post Office from 2024) is testament to Cathy Come Home’s experimentation with the format.

The more pressing reason for its relevance is the endurance of its central theme: homelessness. Numbers of people living in temporary accommodation are unprecedented in recent times: 135,580 households in England – including 177,530 children.

Terrible conditions persist, too. Temporary accommodation is often “unfit for human habitation”, as a government housing committee recently found. This can include homes riddled with damp and mould, or with broken fixtures and fittings, or safety issues. Between 2019 and 2025, temporary accommodation was listed as a contributing factor in the deaths of 104 children.

The film’s enduring impact also rests on the belief that it changed things in British society. For months, newspapers covered their own “Cathy” stories. My recent work with the charity Justlife on temporary accommodation history shows the film wasn’t the first spotlight on these conditions; homeless families had been publicly protesting about their treatment for years. But when the BBC broadcast Cathy’s experiences to 12 million viewers, so many people called in that the switchboard was overwhelmed.

Housing campaign charity Shelter – coincidentally founded two weeks after Cathy Come Home aired – capitalised on the attention by presenting families like Cathy’s in campaign materials and involving actress Carol White in rallies. The charity had raised around £50,000 by 1967 – not all due to Cathy Come Home, but it certainly helped.

The film is also credited with the formation of homelessness charity Crisis in 1967. Politicians even spoke of the drama in parliament, and the minister of housing invited Loach, Sandford and producer Tony Garnett to meet him in Whitehall to discuss the issues it raised.

However, there was no significant change to homelessness law until the Housing (Homeless Persons) Act in 1977 – 11 years after the film. This legally defined homelessness and gave those who met priority-need criteria and were not deemed “intentionally” homeless a right to be rehoused. The law came about primarily due to civil service concerns about how councils were managing homelessness, as well as pressure from housing campaigners. Cathy Come Home was part of that wider story.

Loach and others have credited the film with ending family separation in some areas at the time. Certainly, after a series of public meetings – one of which included Loach, Sandford and homeless families – the council in Birmingham (where parts of the drama were filmed) committed to trying to end family separation within two years. Yet a 1972 Shelter report highlighted the practice continued in the city – and elsewhere. It didn’t end there: an investigation revealed that in 2022-23 at least 50 children were taken into care for the central reason of homelessness.

There were issues with the film’s representation of the period, however. It has been criticised for focusing on the experiences of white homeless people, even though Black and ethnic minority households were more likely to be homeless or living in poor-quality housing.

These concerns remain pertinent. Today, Black-led households are more likely to apply for statutory homelessness support, spend more time in temporary accommodation, and are less likely to be rehoused in social housing than their white counterparts.

Cathy’s family presented the nuclear ideal, too, when unmarried mothers or women fleeing relationship breakdown or domestic violence typically faced much higher barriers to accommodation. Similarly today, single-parent households are nearly four times more likely to be homeless than two-parent families.

Sixty years after Cathy Come Home first aired, many of the problems it depicted remain unresolved. Each anniversary offers a valuable opportunity to hold a mirror up to today and demand affordable, safe and secure housing for everyone. But to do that, we must pay attention to its silences and what it failed to achieve as much as what it depicted.
Jessica Field consulted for Justlife on the report: Lifelines: A history of temporary accommodation in England, 1834-2011.

articles.title: Fjord: 2026 Cannes winner fails to engage with the complexity of Norway’s real child welfare controversies
articles.author: Louis Bayman, Associate Professor in Department of Film Studies, University of Southampton
paras: Written, produced and directed by Romanian film-maker Cristian Mungiu, Fjord won the prestigious Palme d’Or at Cannes in May 2026. The film tells the story of the Gheorghiu family, immigrants from Romania to a remote Norwegian town where they live at the end of the fjord of the film’s title.

Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) are devout evangelical Christians with five equally devout children. They live next door to the headteacher of the local school, Mats Halberg (Markus Tønseth) and his wife Mia (Lisa Carlehed), a lawyer, as well as Mats’ elderly father and teenage daughter from a previous marriage.

When the Gheorghius’ eldest daughter Elia is the subject of a report to social services after her PE teacher spots bruises on her shoulder, all five children are taken into care and the parents put on trial.

Fjord fictionalises several real-life cases that brought international attention to Norway’s child protection laws. Mungiu has described a grander ambition in making Fjord – that of forcing a difficult confrontation with an ethical dilemma: what if the liberals are the real authoritarians?

Mungiu, who also won the Palm d'Or in 2007 with 4 Months, 3 Weeks And 2 Days, belongs to the Romanian New Wave, a group of film-makers whose unflinching realism broke from the orthodoxies of Romanian communism. These strictures required filmmakers to present a positive image of the nation that many felt was increasingly at odds with the truth.

Fjord is Mungiu’s first international film and taps into topics of more global relevance. Complaints of the so-called intolerant left unite the modern right, encapsulating concerns from meddling judges to DEI quotas, cancel culture and mask-wearing.
One dimensional characters

Despite its 147 minutes running time, Fjord struggles to move beyond a political provocation. This would not be a problem if there were some kind of dramatic development, but the film’s characterisations are one-dimensional, without internal conflict or development.

Political filmmaking often embodies antagonistic political positions in its characters – for example the radical classic The Battle of Algiers (1966), or last year’s One Battle After Another. But unlike these films, Fjord refuses either narrative action or political commitment.

Instead, the film adheres to a core generic value of contemporary festival-circuit cinema, that is, ambiguity. Fjord most closely resembles the real 2015 case of the Bodnariu family, where the state took away the five children of a Romanian Christian couple who disciplined their children by slapping them, which is a crime in Norway.

Fjord adds suggestions that Mihai and Lisbet are committing far more violent abuse, presumably because without this there is in reality no uncomfortable ethical dilemma. Norway’s child services have drawn international condemnation for their wildly disproportionate responses to such cases and have been the subject of numerous rulings by the European Court of Human Rights.

Had Fjord instead exhibited genuine suspicion about the parents’ behaviour, it would present a much more difficult proposition about the limits of toleration. But instead the film pulls its punches, dropping the question of physical violence and denying viewers the information they need to know what kind of dilemma is even being posed.

Mungiu describes his film as concerning a “culture clash”, but exhibits similar confusion as to which cultures are actually clashing: the national cultures of Norway and Romania, the ethical worlds of religion and secularism, the generational cultures of tradition and change or the regional cultures of northern and southern Europe.

A film that showed how these factors intersect would be truly impressive, but Fjord is not that film, let down by its fundamental lack of curiosity about the dynamics of the situation it presents. The Gheorghius attend a local evangelical church, but these Christian Norwegians remain mere background detail.

The children drop out of the narrative when the trial beings, meaning we never explore the difficulties of their position. Reinsve is criminally underused as Lisbet, a Norwegian woman adhering to the strict Christianity her husband insists is part of his national belonging as a Romanian.

Criticisms of Fjord have been mischaracterised as centring on its sympathetic presentation of a conservative patriarch. If that were the case then such criticism would also have been made of last year’s Cannes winner It Was Just an Accident, a film about a former torturer who now lives in peace with his wife and family. Such complexity helps in making compelling drama. It is this kind of complexity that the facile unreality of Fjord’s ambiguity rejects.

We may then question whether Fjord, whose funders include the Council of Europe, EU and the Nordic Film Institute, acts as any kind of challenge to liberal pieties at all. No belief system enjoys questioning itself so much as liberalism. Especially if that questioning comes from its right, for this confirms its proclaimed values of tolerance and sophistication.

At the same time, ambiguity, and a reassurance that everything is indeed far too complicated to take a clear stand, flatters the arthouse sensibilities of the festival circuit audience. With all the courage of its own lack of conviction, Fjord does in the end impart a moral lesson: blessed are the uncommitted.

articles.title: Tove Jansson’s illustrations for The Hobbit capture the ‘ecstatic truth’ of childhood
articles.author: Tom Emanuel, PhD, English Literature, University of Glasgow
paras: Long before I knew Finnish-Swedish author and artist Tove Jansson as the creator of the Moomins, I knew her as a name in the margins of The Annotated Hobbit.

Edited by Tolkien scholar Douglas A. Anderson, the book contains explanations of the numerous literary allusions and references to the wider Middle-earth legendarium which dot the landscape of J.R.R. Tolkien’s first novel. It also features more than 150 illustrations from global editions of Tolkien’s beloved classic, including several of Jansson’s for the Swedish translation – En Hobbit’s Äventyr (A Hobbit’s Adventure, 1962).

The recent release of The Hobbit: Illustrated by Tove Jansson marks the first time that a full edition of her Tolkien illustrations has appeared in English. And perhaps now the general reader may understand why my child self was so intrigued by them.

The creator of the Moomins and the maker of Middle-earth may not seem like an obvious pairing, but there are certain parallels between them. Jansson was a Swedish-speaking Finn. Finland’s national epic, The Kalevala (1835), exercised an enormous influence on Tolkien’s legendarium.

Both Tolkien and Jansson’s respective imaginations were fundamentally shaped by Finnish myth and folklore. Moreover, Tolkien heavily borrowed from what he called the “linguistic aesthetics” of Finnish for his invented Elvish language Quenya.

Even bearing this in mind, Jansson’s black-and-white illustrations are very clearly a product of a world before Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings trilogy (2001-2003) set the benchmark for visual adaptations of Tolkien’s work.
From Moominvalley to Middle-earth

In 1962, fantasy had not yet solidified as a distinct publishing genre. It would take the transformation of The Lord of the Rings into a full-blown cultural phenomenon in the late 1960s to do that. This gave artists greater license to interpret The Hobbit as a standalone work of children’s literature, rather than as a prequel to an epic masterpiece.

Jansson did not take The Hobbit’s intended audience as an excuse to “soften” her visualisation of Middle-earth, however. In a 1961 essay, she opined that there is an “intense horror sensation […] in every honest children’s book”. As scholar of children’s literature Olga Holownia has explained: “An opportunity to create horror-infused landscapes was Jansson’s key motivation behind taking on the Tolkien commission. She found the scenery ‘seductive in its macabre ferocity’.”

Jansson’s work on The Hobbit bears this out. Filled with dynamic movement and a sense of the sublime, it showcases a different side of her visual personality, even as its bears her unmistakable artistic imprint.

There is more than a hint of Snufkin (the free-spirited wanderer of her Moomin stories) about her Bilbo in his travelling cloak and out-sized hat. But the Misty Mountains are as far from Moominvalley as it’s possible to get, and the ruined gates of the Lonely Mountain resemble the monstrous jaws of Smaug the dragon himself, with plumes of billowing steam and dragon-fire.

Here and elsewhere, the characters are literally dwarfed by the landscapes they move through and the creatures they meet there. Consider Jansson’s Gollum. Far from a gnarled, shrunken hobbit, he towers over Bilbo like a slimy cave-troll. Those looking for illustrations that precisely match Tolkien’s words will find themselves disappointed. But I would argue that Jansson captured the “ecstatic truth” of being a small person in a vast and imposing world – that is to say, of being a child.

There is no surviving record of Tolkien’s opinion of Jansson’s work. What we do know is that he was iffy on the idea of fantasy illustration at all. In his seminal essay On Fairy-Stories (1947), he wrote:

If a story says ‘he climbed a hill and saw a river in the valley below,’ the illustrator may catch, or nearly catch, his own vision of such a scene; but every hearer of the words will have his own picture, and it will be made out of all the hills and rivers and dales he has ever seen, but especially out of The Hill, The River, The Valley which were for him the first embodiment of the word.

Tolkien’s stated beliefs about visual art and fantasy hardly stopped him from illustrating his own work. Indeed, since The Hobbit’s publication in 1937, Tolkien’s pictures have become all but canonical.

Anyone who has ever watched Hayao Miyazaki’s Spirited Away (2001) or Guillermo del Toro’s Pan’s Labyrinth (2006) – or, for that matter, Jackson’s Lord of the Rings – will know that visual media possess unique enchantments of their own. So, too, does the work of Tove Jansson.

articles.title: Jeremy Latcham takes over as new DC Studios chief: three ways this could play out for the DC universe
articles.author: Roman Pavlyuchenko, Lecturer in Marketing, University of Bath
paras: Hollywood’s superhero industrial complex revolves around DC and Marvel, two huge studios that style themselves as “cinematic universes”. DC owns characters like Batman, Superman and Wonder Woman, while Marvel owns Spider-Man, Captain America and X-Men among others. Problems have been plaguing both studios in recent years, but DC more so.

In April 2026, I wrote that DC Studios president James Gunn was one of the key risk factors for the DC cinematic universe. Building an entire universe around his unique creative vision alone, I argued, could pose serious problems for DC.

The news that Gunn is out as the head of DC Studios after four years seems to have confirmed my hunch. While the director will continue working on the Superman sequel and other films and series slated for 2027, he is being replaced by one-time Marvel veteran Jeremy Latcham.

With such a seismic shift in leadership – and following the huge 2026 box-office flops of Supergirl and Clayface (the horror take on the superhero genre) – what can viewers expect from the DC Cinematic Universe in the coming months and years? Based on my ongoing research into superhero franchises, I see several possible scenarios that could shape the Hollywood studio.
1. Different management, same direction

Gunn is chiefly a director, famous for his quirky action pieces littered with witty dialogue and a penchant for 1980s pop music. Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy (2014-2023) is undoubtedly the best entry into this body of work – films he made before taking on the DC job.

His replacement, Jeremy Latcham, is a producer. One of the earliest employees of Marvel Studios, Latcham helped propel the Marvel cinematic universe to global acclaim with production credits on Iron Man (2008) and The Avengers (2012).
To have a producer and not a director in charge brings in a different skill set to the job, including a certain level of operational excellence required to oversee a cinematic universe.

At the same time, a potential improvement in operational excellence does not address the underlying issues currently affecting the DC universe. For instance, no major villain or narrative direction has been introduced in the new DC Cinematic Universe. Operational excellence is no guarantee of creative and commercial success.
As a complex narrative that would take years to reach a proper dramatic resolution, the DC cinematic universe is currently in disarray.

While 2025’s Superman took viewers into known territory, the other staples of DC comics like Batman, Wonder Woman, or Aquaman are nowhere to be seen. Indeed, no release dates for films about any of these heroes have been confirmed yet. This comes amid one DC project after another being cancelled.

Crucially, the shows and films that have been released do not seem to speak well to one another or the broader DC world. For instance, Clayface, DC’s most recent film makes no direct references to Batman or Superman. It doesn’t even have a post-credits scene – a staple of a good superhero film that sets the scene for what comes next and allows fans to speculate.
In this challenging climate, Latcham’s role may be to clean house and ensure that incoming projects let fans see the DC cinematic universe as a holistic whole worthy of years-long commitment.

It is unlikely that the cancelled projects will be revived. It’s also too late to fix the earlier problems. So Latcham will have to unite and interconnect the projects still on the slate. This seems the most likely scenario.

The “nuclear option” for any expansive narrative is a hard reset, where the existing continuity is brushed aside and a new story universe is created. This is not without precedent in comics, and DC’s recent pivot from their original cinematic universe (2013-2023) proves that the move itself is feasible.

This might also make sense because a new creative direction in an otherwise established continuity may cause more problems than it fixes. Famously, in the previous DC cinematic universe (2013-2023), director Joss Whedon replaced Zack Snyder at the helm of 2017’s Justice League in the middle of post-production.
The switch resulted in a tonally inconsistent film that split the fanbase, forcing DC to release a standalone “Snyder Cut” a few years later.
At the same time, a hard reset may cause a PR crisis given how close it is to the previous reset, which only took place last year when Gunn’s Superman was released.

A proper reset also requires careful thinking about what actually happens afterwards. Here, it appears that the decision to oust Gunn is a fresh one, leaving Latcham little time to figure out major reinventions.

Less than 24 hours after Gunn’s departure, there were already reports that the new management was thinking of rebooting the DC universe again. So while this radical option is an increasing possibility, some serious thinking around long-term planning is required.
Whatever direction DC takes, one thing is clear: replacing Gunn with Latcham is not merely a change in leadership, but potentially a change in how DC thinks about its cinematic universe.

articles.title: How the discovery of a Roman fort rekindled interest in an emperor immortalised in Welsh mythology
articles.author: Aled Ll Jones, Head of School & Reader in Welsh & Medieval Literature, Bangor University
paras: The recent discovery of a Roman timber fort in the Preseli hills of Pembrokeshire, south-west Wales, has brought a medieval Welsh legend into fresh focus.

The site is mentioned in Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig (The Dream of Macsen Wledig), a story about a Roman emperor who travels to Wales. Until now, the account of a camp in that location had largely been treated as a product of medieval imagination. But the archaeological discovery raises an intriguing question: can ancient stories preserve memories of places and events that have been lost to history?

The Dream of Macsen Wledig is one of the 11 medieval Welsh-language tales traditionally grouped together as the Mabinogion. These tales blend history, folklore, magic and legend, while some people see in them lost myths. Featuring kings, warriors, magicians and supernatural beings, the stories offer a glimpse into how people in medieval Wales understood their past and the world around them.

The tales survive in two important Welsh-language manuscripts. First, in Llyfr Gwyn Rhydderch (the White Book of Rhydderch), compiled around the mid-14th century, and second in Llyfr Coch Hergest (the Red Book of Hergest), written towards the end of that century.
But the stories themselves are older. They had been transmitted and copied since before King Edward I’s conquest of Wales in 1282, and perhaps as early as the 11th century.

Five of the tales feature Arthur, the legendary warrior whose tales spread throughout all of Europe. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, are a group of stories spanning the landscapes of Wales, Ireland and England, of this world and the supernatural otherworld. The remaining two, including The Dream of Macsen Wledig, reshape particular strands of early British history through native storytelling. All the tales offer imaginative accounts of power and political authority.
A Roman emperor in Welsh legend

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, a Roman emperor falls in love with a woman he sees in a dream. Determined to find her, he sends messengers to follow the route he has dreamt. Their journey takes them across Europe and eventually to what is now Caernarfon, in north-west Wales.

The emperor is called Macsen Wledig (Macsen the Leader). His character is a literary composite of a number of historical characters, most notably the Galician Magnus Maximus, a Roman general who became Emperor in the late 4th century. Born in a province that is now part of Spain and Portugal, Magnus Maximus seized power in Britain and went on to rule much of the western Roman empire, including Gaul (roughly modern France and neighbouring regions).

His legacy in Wales is particularly significant. In the popular Welsh song Yma o Hyd (Still Here), first released in 1983, the singer and former politician Dafydd Iwan invokes Magnus Maximus’ departure from Britain, supposedly leaving Wales behind as an entire nation.
The song draws on a powerful literary tradition – that the departure of Rome from Britain, just before the arrival of the English, saw the birth of Welsh identity.

But the medieval story is not a straightforward account of historical events. Like the song, it blends historical memory with imagination. Its importance lies not simply in whether every detail is factually accurate, but in what the story tells us about how Welsh people understood the past.

The woman in Macsen’s dream is Elen Luyddog (Elen of the Hosts). She is also a composite character, associated with two figures named Helen or Helena – Helen of Caernarfon and Helena of Constantinople, mother of Constantine the Great. Both were 4th century saints.

In the story, Elen insists that Macsen travel to Wales to marry her. He agrees and she becomes empress. Her father is appointed Viceroy of Britain, and together they begin building powerful fortresses. Elen asks Macsen to establish three towns: Caerllion (Caerleon), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) and Caernarfon.

She also asks him to build roads to link them. Sarn Elen (Elen’s Way) is still the name given to the main Roman road complex linking north and south Wales. The story offers a legendary explanation for features of the landscape that people could still see around them centuries later.
Ancient words, modern truths

One passage in particular in the tale has taken on new significance following the archaeological discovery at Y Frenni Fawr hill in Pembrokeshire. Specifically, the moment in the tale which describes Macsen travelling from Carmarthen to the summit of the hill to hunt. There, he establishes a camp known as Cadair Facsen, or Macsen’s Chair.

Until recently, this reference was generally understood as part of the story’s imaginative landscape. But the discovery of a Roman timber fort on the hill, alongside coins dating from the period of the historical Magnus Maximus, offers a fascinating connection between the medieval account and the archaeological record.

It does not mean that every detail of the story is historically true, but it does suggest that the people who told and recorded the tale may have known about real places and features of the landscape that have since been forgotten. It also raises the possibility that other details in medieval Welsh stories could preserve valuable historical information.

The discovery at Y Frenni Fawr reminds us that the past is not always neatly divided between history and legend. Medieval stories preserve important pieces of older knowledge, even when they have been reshaped over generations. By reading them along with archaeology, linguistics and an eye to the landscape itself, we may discover more about the people who once lived in Wales, the stories they told and how they understood their place in the world. By doing this we understand more about the world we live in today.
